pathway.title: CCO HOLDINGS LLC — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, leverage is steady near 4.2x and drifting up through earnings, not borrowing. CCO HOLDINGS LLC had total debt of USD 93,845 million and net debt of USD 93,560 million at June 30, 2026, which are 4.22x and 4.20x of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA of USD 22,251 million, against 4.17x and 4.16x at December 31, 2024 [CP-1]. Debt fell USD 772 million in the half while last-twelve-months EBITDA fell from USD 22,611 million at FY2025, so the ratio rose from 4.18x. At constant debt, an EBITDA decline of 5%, 10% or 15% would take the ratio to 4.44x, 4.69x or 4.96x (calculated, illustrative). These are principal-debt ratios on company Adjusted EBITDA before the management fees that the covenants add back; they are not the covenant ratios, which the 10-K printed only at December 31, 2025: 4.0x against a 6.0x indenture maximum and 2.8x against 5.0x and 4.0x at Charter Operating [CP-1; Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation].

Second, earnings are eroding on revenue, not cost. Q2 2026 revenue was USD 13,526 million against USD 13,766 million and Adjusted EBITDA USD 5,428 million against USD 5,668 million, a fall of 4.2%; operating costs excluding stock compensation were flat at USD 8,098 million despite USD 65 million of Cox transition expenses [CP-1]. Internet customers fell by 172,000 in the quarter while mobile lines rose by 406,000, Internet revenue fell 3.2% and video revenue 9.7%, and mobile service revenue rose 18.9% [CP-1A]. The business faces fibre overlap from AT&T and Verizon in about 27% and 16% of the footprint and fixed wireless competition [CP-1A]. The mechanism is that a low-lock-in subscription base loses revenue faster than a largely fixed network cost base can adjust, so leverage rises as EBITDA falls (Analyst Interpretation).

Third, cash flow after capital spending is thin and is distributed to the parent. Last-twelve-months free cash flow was USD 5,070 million, or 5.40% of principal debt, after capital expenditure of USD 12,064 million, which is 54.22% of EBITDA [CP-1; calculated]. EBITDA less capital expenditure of USD 10,187 million covers cash interest of USD 5,024 million 2.03x (calculated). Distributions to the parent were USD 5,898 million over the last twelve months and USD 6,794 million in FY2025, against free cash flow of USD 5,070 million and USD 5,827 million, a shortfall of USD 828 million and USD 967 million (calculated); principal debt rose USD 838 million in FY2025 [CP-1]. In the first half of 2026 distributions of USD 2,460 million were close to free cash flow of USD 2,492 million. The 10-Q says the issuer and its subsidiaries are "the primary source" of funding for Charter's buybacks through distributions [CP-1A]. This is a policy choice, limited by an indenture leverage test (4.0x against 6.0x at December 31, 2025) and by Charter's stated 4.0x to 4.5x net leverage range, not by a hard cap (Analyst Interpretation).

Fourth, the unsecured notes are structurally and effectively subordinated, and the layers are thin in turns of EBITDA. Of USD 93,845 million of principal debt, USD 67,111 million (71.5%) is senior secured notes, debentures and credit facilities guaranteed by CCO Holdings and the operating group, and USD 26,734 million is CCO Holdings senior unsecured notes with no subsidiary guarantee [CP-1; CP-1A]. Secured debt is 3.02x of EBITDA and total debt 4.22x, so the unsecured notes occupy the part of the capital structure between 3.02x and 4.22x (calculated). Between December 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026, unsecured notes fell USD 516 million while credit facilities rose USD 504 million, so debt shifted from unsecured to secured [CP-1; CP-1A]. This is a mechanic, not a recovery view: collateral coverage is not computed and executed documents are not supplied.

Fifth, liquidity is adequate and near-term maturities are modest, but refinancing concentrates in 2029 and 2030. Cash of USD 285 million and availability of about USD 3,700 million give liquidity of USD 3,985 million, which is 3.99x the USD 999 million current portion of debt (calculated) [CP-1]. Availability fell from about USD 4,600 million at March 31, 2026 as credit facility debt rose USD 788 million. Scheduled principal was USD 1,055 million for 2026 and USD 3,555 million for 2027 at December 31, 2025; after the February 2026 redemptions of USD 750 million and USD 2,250 million these become USD 305 million and USD 1,305 million before 2026 amortisation already paid and the unallocated repurchases, with 2028 at USD 5,392 million, 2029 at USD 7,279 million and 2030 at USD 13,868 million [CP-1]. The 2029 and 2030 amounts together are USD 21,147 million, 22.35% of year-end principal debt (calculated). The Revolving Loan B of about USD 960 million matures on August 31, 2027, within twelve months of the as-of date, and the equipment installment plan facility's revolving period is subject to renewal around the as-of date (inference from the November 2025 amendment) [CP-1].

Sixth, refinancing and floating-rate exposure raise cost over time. The 87% of debt that was fixed at December 31, 2025 had an average rate of 5.07%, and the 13% that floats had a forward-implied average of 5.36%; Item 7A describes only cross-currency swaps on the sterling notes and no interest rate derivatives (10-K page:105). A 1.00% move on the USD 12,453 million of credit facility debt would change annual interest by about USD 125 million, 2.5% of last-twelve-months cash interest of USD 5,024 million (calculated, before floors). The January 2026 notes carry 7.000% and 7.375% coupons against 5.500% and 5.125% on the USD 3,000 million redeemed, an annual coupon increase of about USD 58 million before the interest saved on the USD 1,249 million of repurchases, whose coupons are not disclosed (calculated). The 10-K scheduled USD 4,817 million of interest for 2026 and USD 4,646 million for 2027 on the year-end debt before those events (10-K page:160).

Seventh, the Cox Transactions and the Liberty Broadband Combination are the largest open items. The issuer's 10-Q expects Cox's unsecured notes to become guaranteed and secured debt, Cox entities to become Obligors and all or part of about USD 4.2 billion of new debt to do the same; the cash consideration is USD 4.0 billion in the 10-K and about USD 4.2 billion in the 2026 10-Qs, which tracks Charter Holdings' cash payment moving from USD 500 million to USD 650 million, and the assumed Cox net debt and finance leases are USD 12.4 billion in the 10-Qs and USD 12.6 billion on a pro forma basis in the 10-K [CP-1A]. The filings do not say where Cox earnings will sit relative to the issuer, who issues the new debt, or whether any approval has been received. That is a missing datapoint, not an adverse finding; it decides whether the issuer's secured layer grows while its own EBITDA base does not (Insufficient Information and Analyst Interpretation).

Eighth, covenant headroom looks wide at the last printed date but cannot be measured now. At December 31, 2025 the indenture leverage of 4.0x was 2.0 turns below the 6.0x maximum, and the Charter Operating ratios of 2.8x were 2.2 turns and 1.2 turns below the 5.0x total and 4.0x first lien tests, equivalent to EBITDA cushions of about 33%, 44% and 30% at constant debt (calculated from rounded ratios) [CP-1]. A proxy using Adjusted EBITDA plus management fees of about USD 1,400 million gives 2.81x for secured debt and 3.94x for total debt, close to the printed figures. No ratio is printed after December 31, 2025 and definitions and baskets are not supplied (Insufficient Information).

cells.text: Broadband connectivity company: Spectrum Internet, Mobile, TV and Voice for residential and small to large business customers; "nearly 59 million homes and small to large businesses across 41 states" at June 30, 2026 (58 million at December 31, 2025).
Scale across a wide footprint; revenue is not tied to one region.

About 89% of revenue in FY2025 and FY2024 is monthly subscription fees for Internet, mobile, video, voice and commercial services plus regional sports and news channels; subscriptions can generally be discontinued at any time. The other 11% is advertising, franchise and regulatory fees collected for authorities, device sales, processing and installation fees and similar.
Recurring revenue is high, but low contractual lock-in means customer losses reduce revenue quickly.

Internet 23,765, mobile service 3,762, video 13,703, voice 1,350, commercial 7,315, advertising 1,468, other 3,411 of 54,774; residential revenue 42,580. Internet is 43.39%, video 25.02%, mobile 6.87% (calculated).
Video is a quarter of revenue and declining; Internet is the largest line.

Q2 2026 revenue 13,526 against 13,766: Internet 5,776 against 5,969 (down 3.2%), video 3,149 against 3,488 (down 9.7%), mobile service 1,095 against 921 (up 18.9%), commercial 1,865 against 1,836, advertising 416 against 371.
Mobile and commercial growth offset only part of Internet and video decline.

June 30, 2026 against June 30, 2025 (thousands): customer relationships 31,499 against 32,060; Internet 29,388 against 29,908; mobile lines 12,540 against 10,856; video 12,524 against 12,631; voice 5,694 against 6,386. In Q2 2026 Internet fell 172,000 and mobile lines rose 406,000.
Penetration is falling in the core product; mobile growth is the offset.

Standardised Spectrum pricing and bundles with multi-year guaranteed pricing and speed options, moving from "lower promotional and persistent bundled pricing" to drive growth. Monthly residential revenue per residential customer was $117.52 against $119.70 (down 1.8%, calculated).
10-K page:16 to page:17; 10-Q Jun 2026 page:18 to page:19
Pricing is being used to defend volume, so revenue per customer is not rising.

Programming costs were 2,035 against 2,253 in Q2 2026, 25% against 27% of operating costs; costs allocated to programmer streaming applications are netted within video revenue (184 in Q2). Media consolidation has given programmers "additional selling power".
Programming cost falls with customers and the allocation, so video revenue decline is partly cost-neutral.

Spectrum Mobile uses customers' WiFi, 49 million out-of-home WiFi access points and the Verizon cellular network; a July 2025 agreement with T-Mobile US, Inc. is set to deliver mobile services to Spectrum Business customers from 2026; customers can pay for devices under interest-free monthly installment plans financed through the equipment installment plan facility.
10-K page:10, page:17; 10-Q Jun 2026 page:11 to page:13
Mobile depends on a third-party network and device financing, adding working capital and secured borrowing (CP-1).

Spectrum Business (small business, and mid-market and large business including wholesale to carriers), Spectrum Reach advertising, regional sports networks (Los Angeles Lakers rights through 2032; SportsNet LA affiliate and advertising agreements through 2038; a 35.0% interest in Sterling Entertainment Enterprises, LLC), over 35 local news channels and Spectrum Community Solutions.
Diversifies revenue; sports rights are long fixed commitments.

AT&T and Verizon are the primary fiber-to-the-home competitors with overlap in approximately 27% and 16% of the operating footprint; fixed wireless, satellite, DSL, virtual MVPDs and direct broadcast satellite also compete; national mobile operators are expanding 5G and converged offers.
Competitive intensity explains the Internet customer losses and caps pricing.

Hybrid fiber coaxial network with a network evolution programme (1.2 GHz then 1.8 GHz spectrum, high split, DAA, DOCSIS 4.0) "largely complete by the end of 2027"; capital expenditure was 11,624 in FY2025 and 5,713 in 6M 2026, and about 11.4 billion is expected for 2026 excluding Cox.
10-K page:6 to page:7, page:18; 10-Q Jun 2026 page:37
A fixed capital programme absorbs cash that would otherwise reduce debt (CP-1).

Since 2022 the issuer has spent $7.7 billion and activated about 1.3 million passings; it expects to invest over $8 billion in total, of which over $2 billion of support has been awarded; failure to meet build-out milestones "could subject us to financial penalties". Spend was 391 in Q2 2026 and 818 in 6M 2026.
Capital is committed ahead of subsidy receipt and carries milestone penalty risk.

Q2 2026 operating costs and expenses 8,236: programming 2,035, other costs of revenue 1,837, field and technology operations 1,313, customer operations 785, marketing and residential sales 927, stock compensation 138, Cox transition expenses 65, other 1,136. Over 80% of customer premise service transactions are handled by the in-house field workforce; about 91,900 full-time equivalent employees at December 31, 2025.
Costs are largely fixed in the short run; transition costs rise ahead of Cox.

Accounts receivable, net 3,580 and accrued capital expenditures 3,162 at June 30, 2026; equipment installment plan receivables of about 1.4 billion current and 1.2 billion noncurrent; supply chain finance obligations 725 and deferred payment program 1,155.
10-Q Jun 2026 page:5, page:9 to page:10, page:13
Vendor and device financing extend payables and receivables; both are claims outside the debt figure (CP-1).

Cable franchises are non-exclusive and not guaranteed to renew; retransmission consent and pole attachment rules affect video costs and rural construction; federal pole rules apply in twenty-six states.
Franchise loss or higher regulated costs hit local revenue and costs.

Franchises 67,471 and goodwill 29,710 are 97,181 of 153,439 total assets at June 30, 2026 (63.34%, calculated). The fourth quarter 2025 impairment analysis found franchise fair value above carrying value "by more than 10%" in each unit; management is monitoring the decline in Charter's stock price.
Equity cushion is intangible-heavy; an impairment would not change cash flow but could affect covenants defined on book values (not supplied).
In the fourth quarter of 2025 customer statistics were revised to include mobile-only customers and a connectivity customer measure, and prior periods were revised.
Customer series before the revision are not directly comparable to older filings.
"Our business is subject to seasonal and cyclical variations": seasonal customers in college and vacation service areas, and cyclical advertising patterns and viewership levels.
Seasonality is stated as a risk without quantification; advertising revenue is the cyclical line (Q2 2026 advertising 416).
No single-customer concentration or contract backlog is disclosed in the sources searched.
Absence of disclosure is not a conclusion; revenue is retail and subscription based.

runs.text: Strengths. (1) Scale and stable margin: USD 22,251 million of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA at a 40.91% margin across 41 states, with revenue of USD 54,396 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1, CP-1A). (2) Debt service capacity: cash interest cover of 4.43x and EBITDA less capital expenditure covering cash interest 2.03x (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (3) Liquidity and a long-dated profile: USD 3,985 million of liquidity, USD 305 million and USD 1,305 million of scheduled principal for 2026 and 2027 after the February 2026 redemptions, and 67.08% of year-end principal debt due after 2030 (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (4) Mostly fixed-rate debt: 87% of principal at year-end, which limits rate sensitivity to about USD 125 million per 1.00% on the floating part (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (5) Visible covenant room at the last printed date: 4.0x against 6.0x and 2.8x against 5.0x and 4.0x at December 31, 2025 (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (6) Growth segments: mobile lines up 1,684 thousand over twelve months and mobile service revenue up 18.9% in Q2 2026 (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). (7) Clean audited disclosure: an unqualified KPMG LLP opinion on FY2025 and regular debt, guarantor and reconciliation disclosure (Documentary Fact; CP-1A).

Weaknesses. (1) Leverage above 4x and rising slowly: 4.22x on debt and 4.34x including the equipment installment plan facility and short-term borrowings, with Adjusted EBITDA down 4.2% in Q2 2026 (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (2) Cash leakage above free cash flow: USD 5,898 million of distributions against USD 5,070 million over the last twelve months, and free cash flow down to USD 2,492 million from USD 3,249 million in the half (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (3) Subordinated unsecured notes: USD 26,734 million behind USD 67,111 million of secured debt, with debt shifting toward secured credit facilities in 2026 (Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation; CP-1, CP-1A). (4) Refinancing concentration and cost: USD 21,147 million due in 2029 and 2030 and about USD 58 million more annual coupon on the early 2026 refinancing (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (5) Capital intensity and intangible-heavy assets: capital expenditure of USD 12,064 million is 54.22% of EBITDA, and franchises and goodwill are 63.34% of total assets, with a fair-value cushion of more than 10% at the last impairment test (Documentary Fact; CP-1, CP-1A). (6) Competition and customer losses: Internet and video customers falling against fibre and fixed wireless entrants (Documentary Fact and Management Language; CP-1A). (7) Opaque post-closing structure and missing documents: Cox financing, perimeter and approvals not supplied; indentures, credit agreement and covenant definitions not supplied (Insufficient Information; CP-0, CP-1A). (8) Claims outside debt of USD 1,596 million of equipment installment plan financing and USD 1,155 million of short-term borrowings, USD 725 million of supply chain finance and USD 1,276 million of operating leases that are not in the debt figure (Documentary Fact; CP-1).

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: The principal transaction is the pending Cox acquisition by Charter and Charter Holdings, not by the issuer. On May 16, 2025, Charter, Charter Holdings and Cox Enterprises, Inc. entered into a Transaction Agreement under which Charter buys 100% of certain Cox Communications subsidiaries that conduct its commercial fiber and managed IT and cloud services businesses, and Cox Enterprises contributes Cox Communications' residential cable business to Charter Holdings, with Cox Enterprises paying $1.00 for a new class of Charter Class C common stock (10-Q Jun 2026 page:8). Consideration is 3.5 billion in cash from Charter for the equity sale and, for the contribution, cash from Charter Holdings plus convertible preferred units of Charter Holdings with a 6.0 billion liquidation preference paying 6.875% and about 33.6 million Charter Holdings common units; the cash from Charter Holdings is 650 million in the 2026 10-Qs and 500 million in the 10-K and the Q3 2025 10-Q (10-Q Jun 2026 page:9; 10-K page:28; 10-Q Sep 2025 page:9). The combined entity will assume Cox Communications' approximately 12.4 billion of net debt and finance leases (10-Q Jun 2026 page:9), a figure the 10-K gave as approximately 12.6 billion on a pro forma basis for Cox refinancings between signing and closing (10-K page:28). The status is pending: the June 2026 10-Q uses the future tense throughout, lists the ability to satisfy closing conditions among its risks and gives no closing date; the 10-K lists conditions including Charter stockholder approvals, expiry of the Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period and approvals of the Federal Communications Commission and certain local franchise, state franchising and state public utility commission authorities (10-K page:61). Which approvals have been received, the end date and the termination fee amounts are not in the pack (the 10-K says only that Charter "could owe a substantial termination fee" (10-K page:62)).

For creditors the key text is the issuer's own: the 10-Q says the company is "also required to fund approximately $4.2 billion of cash purchase price at the closing of the Cox Transactions" (10-Q Jun 2026 page:27), while the 10-K says "Charter is obligated to fund $4.0 billion of cash consideration under the Transaction Agreement which we expect to fund by incurring indebtedness" (10-K page:64). After closing the issuer "presently expect[s]" that Cox's unsecured notes assumed at closing "will constitute Guaranteed and Secured Debt", that Cox Communications and substantially all of its subsidiaries "will become Obligors", and that all or part of the approximately 4.2 billion of indebtedness issued to finance the cash payment "may constitute Guaranteed and Secured Debt when issued" (10-Q Jun 2026 page:34). Charter and its subsidiaries, including CCO Holdings, are also subject to restrictions on the conduct of their business before closing, including in certain cases the ability to incur certain indebtedness (10-K page:65). The contribution is to Charter Holdings (10-Q Jun 2026 page:8), and the filings do not say whether Cox's operating results will be consolidated in CCO Holdings' statements after closing or sit elsewhere in Charter's structure. That is Insufficient Information, not an adverse conclusion; it matters because Cox debt could be guaranteed inside the Obligor Group, which the issuer guarantees, while Cox earnings might not be in the issuer's own statements. The cash-purchase financing is described only as debt to be incurred; no sources and uses, commitment papers, rating agency actions or liquidity effect are given. Cox transition costs are already in operating results (65 in Q2 2026 and 89 in 6M 2026) with 34 and 37 of transition capital expenditure (10-Q Jun 2026 page:14 to page:15, page:37).

The second pending transaction is the Liberty Broadband Combination, a merger agreement dated November 12, 2024 under which Charter acquires Liberty Broadband Corporation through a merger and upstream merger, with Liberty Broadband becoming a wholly owned subsidiary of Charter (10-Q Jun 2026 page:28). Pending its closing, Charter buys Charter Class A shares from Liberty Broadband monthly, and in May 2026 Charter advanced a term loan of approximately 359 million to Liberty Broadband (10-Q Jun 2026 page:29 to page:30). The 10-K expects additional debt "in connection with the Cox Transactions and Liberty Broadband Combination" and the assumption of indebtedness of Liberty Broadband and its subsidiaries (10-K page:52). The amount and ranking of any Liberty Broadband debt are not stated.

New debt issues in the periods covered: in September 2025 Charter Operating and Charter Communications Operating Capital Corp. jointly issued 1.25 billion of 5.850% senior secured notes due December 2035 at 99.932% and 750 million of 6.700% senior secured notes due December 2055 at 99.832%, with proceeds used for general corporate purposes including repayment of the 6.150% senior secured notes due 2026 and potential buybacks, and a loss on extinguishment of about 28 million (10-K page:155). In January 2026 CCO Holdings and CCO Holdings Capital Corp. jointly issued 1.75 billion of 7.000% senior notes due February 2033 and 1.25 billion of 7.375% senior notes due February 2036, both at par, with proceeds for general corporate purposes including the call of 750 million of the 5.500% notes due 2026 and part (2.25 billion) of the 5.125% notes due 2027 (10-K page:155; 10-Q Mar 2026 page:11). In November 2025 the equipment installment plan facility was amended to extend maturity to November 3, 2029 and raise capacity to 2.0 billion (10-K page:161). In the second quarter of 2026 the company repurchased 1.2 billion of principal of various series on the open market at a gain of about 243 million (10-Q Jun 2026 page:11). No new notes are reported for the first half of 2026 other than the January issuance, and no source reports issuance after June 30, 2026.

fields.value: Consistency with CP-0 and CP-1: this answer confirms both and refines two points. First, CP-0 and CP-1 logged the Cox cash figures of 4.0 billion (10-K) and 4.2 billion (10-Qs) without a source for the difference, and CP-0 said the components in the 10-Q do not equal 4.0 billion. The sources do explain it: the cash component payable by Charter Holdings is 500 in the Q3 2025 10-Q and the 10-K and 650 in the Q1 and Q2 2026 10-Qs, so 3,500 + 500 = 4,000 and 3,500 + 650 = 4,150, which the 2026 10-Qs round to 4.2 billion. The filings do not say why it changed. Second, the 12.6 billion assumed Cox net debt in the 10-K is stated "on a pro forma basis contemplating Cox Communications refinancing of debt maturities occurring between signing and closing", while the Q3 2025 and 2026 10-Qs give 12.4 billion without that qualifier; CP-1 reported both without this explanation. The 10-K also states that Charter, not the issuer, "is obligated to fund $4.0 billion of cash consideration" (10-K page:64), which narrows the payer question CP-1 left open (the new indebtedness issuer is still not stated). No figure in CP-0 or CP-1 is changed.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CCO Holdings is a holding company whose principal assets are the equity of its operating subsidiaries, which deliver Spectrum Internet, Mobile, TV and Voice to residential and business customers in 41 states under a single reportable segment. It is wholly owned by CCH I Holdings, LLC and sits inside Charter's chain; it has no sponsor, no listed equity and no public ownership of its own. Its business is a mature, subscription-based, capital-intensive network operator: about 89% of revenue is monthly subscription fees, residential revenue is 77.74% of FY2025 revenue, and revenue is drifting down slightly (Q2 2026 revenue 13,526 against 13,766) because Internet and video customers are eroding faster than mobile lines and commercial revenue grow. The creditor-relevant structure is the more important feature. Of the issuer's 93,845 of principal debt at June 30, 2026, 67,111 is secured and guaranteed by the issuer and the operating group, while its own 26,734 of unsecured notes are structurally and effectively subordinated, and the issuer's subsidiaries are the primary funding source for Charter's buybacks through distributions. The transaction that matters is the pending Cox acquisition by Charter and Charter Holdings: the issuer's filings say Cox's unsecured notes are expected to become guaranteed and secured debt and Cox entities to become Obligors, which would add claims ahead of the issuer's unsecured notes while the filings do not show where Cox's earnings will sit. The Liberty Broadband Combination is a second pending parent-level transaction. Nothing is supplied after July 24, 2026, so closing status, Cox financing and any new issuance since June are unknown.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The principal transaction is the pending Cox acquisition by Charter and Charter Holdings, not by the issuer. On May 16, 2025, Charter, Charter Holdings and Cox Enterprises, Inc. entered into a Transaction Agreement under which Charter buys 100% of certain Cox Communications subsidiaries that conduct its commercial fiber and managed IT and cloud services businesses, and Cox Enterprises contributes Cox Communications' residential cable business to Charter Holdings, with Cox Enterprises paying $1.00 for a new class of Charter Class C common stock (10-Q Jun 2026 page:8). Consideration is 3.5 billion in cash from Charter for the equity sale and, for the contribution, cash from Charter Holdings plus convertible preferred units of Charter Holdings with a 6.0 billion liquidation preference paying 6.875% and about 33.6 million Charter Holdings common units; the cash from Charter Holdings is 650 million in the 2026 10-Qs and 500 million in the 10-K and the Q3 2025 10-Q (10-Q Jun 2026 page:9; 10-K page:28; 10-Q Sep 2025 page:9). The combined entity will assume Cox Communications' approximately 12.4 billion of net debt and finance leases (10-Q Jun 2026 page:9), a figure the 10-K gave as approximately 12.6 billion on a pro forma basis for Cox refinancings between signing and closing (10-K page:28). The status is pending: the June 2026 10-Q uses the future tense throughout, lists the ability to satisfy closing conditions among its risks and gives no closing date; the 10-K lists conditions including Charter stockholder approvals, expiry of the Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period and approvals of the Federal Communications Commission and certain local franchise, state franchising and state public utility commission authorities (10-K page:61). Which approvals have been received, the end date and the termination fee amounts are not in the pack (the 10-K says only that Charter "could owe a substantial termination fee" (10-K page:62)).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: For creditors the key text is the issuer's own: the 10-Q says the company is "also required to fund approximately $4.2 billion of cash purchase price at the closing of the Cox Transactions" (10-Q Jun 2026 page:27), while the 10-K says "Charter is obligated to fund $4.0 billion of cash consideration under the Transaction Agreement which we expect to fund by incurring indebtedness" (10-K page:64). After closing the issuer "presently expect[s]" that Cox's unsecured notes assumed at closing "will constitute Guaranteed and Secured Debt", that Cox Communications and substantially all of its subsidiaries "will become Obligors", and that all or part of the approximately 4.2 billion of indebtedness issued to finance the cash payment "may constitute Guaranteed and Secured Debt when issued" (10-Q Jun 2026 page:34). Charter and its subsidiaries, including CCO Holdings, are also subject to restrictions on the conduct of their business before closing, including in certain cases the ability to incur certain indebtedness (10-K page:65). The contribution is to Charter Holdings (10-Q Jun 2026 page:8), and the filings do not say whether Cox's operating results will be consolidated in CCO Holdings' statements after closing or sit elsewhere in Charter's structure. That is Insufficient Information, not an adverse conclusion; it matters because Cox debt could be guaranteed inside the Obligor Group, which the issuer guarantees, while Cox earnings might not be in the issuer's own statements. The cash-purchase financing is described only as debt to be incurred; no sources and uses, commitment papers, rating agency actions or liquidity effect are given. Cox transition costs are already in operating results (65 in Q2 2026 and 89 in 6M 2026) with 34 and 37 of transition capital expenditure (10-Q Jun 2026 page:14 to page:15, page:37).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The second pending transaction is the Liberty Broadband Combination, a merger agreement dated November 12, 2024 under which Charter acquires Liberty Broadband Corporation through a merger and upstream merger, with Liberty Broadband becoming a wholly owned subsidiary of Charter (10-Q Jun 2026 page:28). Pending its closing, Charter buys Charter Class A shares from Liberty Broadband monthly, and in May 2026 Charter advanced a term loan of approximately 359 million to Liberty Broadband (10-Q Jun 2026 page:29 to page:30). The 10-K expects additional debt "in connection with the Cox Transactions and Liberty Broadband Combination" and the assumption of indebtedness of Liberty Broadband and its subsidiaries (10-K page:52). The amount and ranking of any Liberty Broadband debt are not stated.

In January 2026 CCO Holdings and CCO Holdings Capital Corp. jointly issued 1.75 billion of 7.000% senior notes due February 2033 and 1.25 billion of 7.375% senior notes due February 2036, both at par, with proceeds for general corporate purposes including the call of 750 million of the 5.500% notes due 2026 and part (2.25 billion) of the 5.125% notes due 2027 (10-K page:155; 10-Q Mar 2026 page:11). In November 2025 the equipment installment plan facility was amended to extend maturity to November 3, 2029 and raise capacity to 2.0 billion (10-K page:161). In the second quarter of 2026 the company repurchased 1.2 billion of principal of various series on the open market at a gain of about 243 million (10-Q Jun 2026 page:11). No new notes are reported for the first half of 2026 other than the January issuance, and no source reports issuance after June 30, 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Locators in tables are `page:N` of the pinned `.jsonl` text, not printed page numbers. Consistency with upstream: this answer agrees with CP-0, CP-1 and CP-1A and corrects none. It adds the 10-K Item 7A table of fixed and variable rate debt by maturity year (10-K page:105), which confirms the variable-rate maturity components that CP-1 had derived by difference (642 in 2028, 279 in 2029, 8,068 in 2030) and the finding that the Revolving Loan B was undrawn at year-end (variable-rate 2027 maturities of 305 equal the term loan amortisation alone). It also adds a few new calculations, all shown below.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CCO HOLDINGS LLC is a large, cash-generative but leveraged cable credit whose earnings are eroding slowly and whose structure and pending acquisition decide its direction. The strongest support is USD 22,251 million of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA at a 40.91% margin, cash interest cover of 4.43x and liquidity of USD 3,985 million, with little principal due before 2028. The weakest point is USD 93,845 million of debt at 4.22x, of which USD 26,734 million of unsecured notes sit behind USD 67,111 million of secured debt (3.02x), while distributions to the parent exceeded free cash flow. What decides the outcome is the Cox closing: how it is financed, whether Cox debt joins the guaranteed and secured group, and the parent's leverage policy afterwards. None of that is in the sources after July 24, 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, leverage is steady near 4.2x and drifting up through earnings, not borrowing. CCO HOLDINGS LLC had total debt of USD 93,845 million and net debt of USD 93,560 million at June 30, 2026, which are 4.22x and 4.20x of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA of USD 22,251 million, against 4.17x and 4.16x at December 31, 2024 [CP-1]. Debt fell USD 772 million in the half while last-twelve-months EBITDA fell from USD 22,611 million at FY2025, so the ratio rose from 4.18x. At constant debt, an EBITDA decline of 5%, 10% or 15% would take the ratio to 4.44x, 4.69x or 4.96x (calculated, illustrative). These are principal-debt ratios on company Adjusted EBITDA before the management fees that the covenants add back; they are not the covenant ratios, which the 10-K printed only at December 31, 2025: 4.0x against a 6.0x indenture maximum and 2.8x against 5.0x and 4.0x at Charter Operating [CP-1; Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Second, earnings are eroding on revenue, not cost. Q2 2026 revenue was USD 13,526 million against USD 13,766 million and Adjusted EBITDA USD 5,428 million against USD 5,668 million, a fall of 4.2%; operating costs excluding stock compensation were flat at USD 8,098 million despite USD 65 million of Cox transition expenses [CP-1]. Internet customers fell by 172,000 in the quarter while mobile lines rose by 406,000, Internet revenue fell 3.2% and video revenue 9.7%, and mobile service revenue rose 18.9% [CP-1A]. The business faces fibre overlap from AT&T and Verizon in about 27% and 16% of the footprint and fixed wireless competition [CP-1A]. The mechanism is that a low-lock-in subscription base loses revenue faster than a largely fixed network cost base can adjust, so leverage rises as EBITDA falls (Analyst Interpretation).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, cash flow after capital spending is thin and is distributed to the parent. Last-twelve-months free cash flow was USD 5,070 million, or 5.40% of principal debt, after capital expenditure of USD 12,064 million, which is 54.22% of EBITDA [CP-1; calculated]. EBITDA less capital expenditure of USD 10,187 million covers cash interest of USD 5,024 million 2.03x (calculated). Distributions to the parent were USD 5,898 million over the last twelve months and USD 6,794 million in FY2025, against free cash flow of USD 5,070 million and USD 5,827 million, a shortfall of USD 828 million and USD 967 million (calculated); principal debt rose USD 838 million in FY2025 [CP-1]. In the first half of 2026 distributions of USD 2,460 million were close to free cash flow of USD 2,492 million. The 10-Q says the issuer and its subsidiaries are "the primary source" of funding for Charter's buybacks through distributions [CP-1A]. This is a policy choice, limited by an indenture leverage test (4.0x against 6.0x at December 31, 2025) and by Charter's stated 4.0x to 4.5x net leverage range, not by a hard cap (Analyst Interpretation).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, the unsecured notes are structurally and effectively subordinated, and the layers are thin in turns of EBITDA. Of USD 93,845 million of principal debt, USD 67,111 million (71.5%) is senior secured notes, debentures and credit facilities guaranteed by CCO Holdings and the operating group, and USD 26,734 million is CCO Holdings senior unsecured notes with no subsidiary guarantee [CP-1; CP-1A]. Secured debt is 3.02x of EBITDA and total debt 4.22x, so the unsecured notes occupy the part of the capital structure between 3.02x and 4.22x (calculated). Between December 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026, unsecured notes fell USD 516 million while credit facilities rose USD 504 million, so debt shifted from unsecured to secured [CP-1; CP-1A]. This is a mechanic, not a recovery view: collateral coverage is not computed and executed documents are not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, liquidity is adequate and near-term maturities are modest, but refinancing concentrates in 2029 and 2030. Cash of USD 285 million and availability of about USD 3,700 million give liquidity of USD 3,985 million, which is 3.99x the USD 999 million current portion of debt (calculated) [CP-1]. Availability fell from about USD 4,600 million at March 31, 2026 as credit facility debt rose USD 788 million. Scheduled principal was USD 1,055 million for 2026 and USD 3,555 million for 2027 at December 31, 2025; after the February 2026 redemptions of USD 750 million and USD 2,250 million these become USD 305 million and USD 1,305 million before 2026 amortisation already paid and the unallocated repurchases, with 2028 at USD 5,392 million, 2029 at USD 7,279 million and 2030 at USD 13,868 million [CP-1]. The 2029 and 2030 amounts together are USD 21,147 million, 22.35% of year-end principal debt (calculated). The Revolving Loan B of about USD 960 million matures on August 31, 2027, within twelve months of the as-of date, and the equipment installment plan facility's revolving period is subject to renewal around the as-of date (inference from the November 2025 amendment) [CP-1].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Sixth, refinancing and floating-rate exposure raise cost over time. The 87% of debt that was fixed at December 31, 2025 had an average rate of 5.07%, and the 13% that floats had a forward-implied average of 5.36%; Item 7A describes only cross-currency swaps on the sterling notes and no interest rate derivatives (10-K page:105). A 1.00% move on the USD 12,453 million of credit facility debt would change annual interest by about USD 125 million, 2.5% of last-twelve-months cash interest of USD 5,024 million (calculated, before floors). The January 2026 notes carry 7.000% and 7.375% coupons against 5.500% and 5.125% on the USD 3,000 million redeemed, an annual coupon increase of about USD 58 million before the interest saved on the USD 1,249 million of repurchases, whose coupons are not disclosed (calculated). The 10-K scheduled USD 4,817 million of interest for 2026 and USD 4,646 million for 2027 on the year-end debt before those events (10-K page:160).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Seventh, the Cox Transactions and the Liberty Broadband Combination are the largest open items. The issuer's 10-Q expects Cox's unsecured notes to become guaranteed and secured debt, Cox entities to become Obligors and all or part of about USD 4.2 billion of new debt to do the same; the cash consideration is USD 4.0 billion in the 10-K and about USD 4.2 billion in the 2026 10-Qs, which tracks Charter Holdings' cash payment moving from USD 500 million to USD 650 million, and the assumed Cox net debt and finance leases are USD 12.4 billion in the 10-Qs and USD 12.6 billion on a pro forma basis in the 10-K [CP-1A]. The filings do not say where Cox earnings will sit relative to the issuer, who issues the new debt, or whether any approval has been received. That is a missing datapoint, not an adverse finding; it decides whether the issuer's secured layer grows while its own EBITDA base does not (Insufficient Information and Analyst Interpretation).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Eighth, covenant headroom looks wide at the last printed date but cannot be measured now. At December 31, 2025 the indenture leverage of 4.0x was 2.0 turns below the 6.0x maximum, and the Charter Operating ratios of 2.8x were 2.2 turns and 1.2 turns below the 5.0x total and 4.0x first lien tests, equivalent to EBITDA cushions of about 33%, 44% and 30% at constant debt (calculated from rounded ratios) [CP-1]. A proxy using Adjusted EBITDA plus management fees of about USD 1,400 million gives 2.81x for secured debt and 3.94x for total debt, close to the printed figures. No ratio is printed after December 31, 2025 and definitions and baskets are not supplied (Insufficient Information).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. (1) Scale and stable margin: USD 22,251 million of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA at a 40.91% margin across 41 states, with revenue of USD 54,396 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1, CP-1A). (2) Debt service capacity: cash interest cover of 4.43x and EBITDA less capital expenditure covering cash interest 2.03x (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (3) Liquidity and a long-dated profile: USD 3,985 million of liquidity, USD 305 million and USD 1,305 million of scheduled principal for 2026 and 2027 after the February 2026 redemptions, and 67.08% of year-end principal debt due after 2030 (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (4) Mostly fixed-rate debt: 87% of principal at year-end, which limits rate sensitivity to about USD 125 million per 1.00% on the floating part (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (5) Visible covenant room at the last printed date: 4.0x against 6.0x and 2.8x against 5.0x and 4.0x at December 31, 2025 (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (6) Growth segments: mobile lines up 1,684 thousand over twelve months and mobile service revenue up 18.9% in Q2 2026 (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). (7) Clean audited disclosure: an unqualified KPMG LLP opinion on FY2025 and regular debt, guarantor and reconciliation disclosure (Documentary Fact; CP-1A).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. (1) Leverage above 4x and rising slowly: 4.22x on debt and 4.34x including the equipment installment plan facility and short-term borrowings, with Adjusted EBITDA down 4.2% in Q2 2026 (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (2) Cash leakage above free cash flow: USD 5,898 million of distributions against USD 5,070 million over the last twelve months, and free cash flow down to USD 2,492 million from USD 3,249 million in the half (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (3) Subordinated unsecured notes: USD 26,734 million behind USD 67,111 million of secured debt, with debt shifting toward secured credit facilities in 2026 (Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation; CP-1, CP-1A). (4) Refinancing concentration and cost: USD 21,147 million due in 2029 and 2030 and about USD 58 million more annual coupon on the early 2026 refinancing (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (5) Capital intensity and intangible-heavy assets: capital expenditure of USD 12,064 million is 54.22% of EBITDA, and franchises and goodwill are 63.34% of total assets, with a fair-value cushion of more than 10% at the last impairment test (Documentary Fact; CP-1, CP-1A). (6) Competition and customer losses: Internet and video customers falling against fibre and fixed wireless entrants (Documentary Fact and Management Language; CP-1A). (7) Opaque post-closing structure and missing documents: Cox financing, perimeter and approvals not supplied; indentures, credit agreement and covenant definitions not supplied (Insufficient Information; CP-0, CP-1A). (8) Claims outside debt of USD 1,596 million of equipment installment plan financing and USD 1,155 million of short-term borrowings, USD 725 million of supply chain finance and USD 1,276 million of operating leases that are not in the debt figure (Documentary Fact; CP-1).
